claim: Beta-catenin (canonical Wnt) signaling controls CNS angiogenesis.
source: Beta-catenin (i.e., canonical Wnt) signaling controls CNS angiogenesis and the blood-brain and blood-retina barriers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: Beta-catenin signaling controls the blood-brain and blood-retina barriers.
source: Beta-catenin (i.e., canonical Wnt) signaling controls CNS angiogenesis and the blood-brain and blood-retina barriers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: EC-specific loss of Dlg1 produces a retinal vascular phenotype that closely matches the phenotype associated with reduced beta-catenin signaling.
source: EC-specific loss of Dlg1 produces a retinal vascular phenotype that closely matches the phenotype associated with reduced beta-catenin signaling, synergizes with genetically-directed reductions in beta-catenin signaling components, and can be rescued by stabilizing beta-catenin in ECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing phenotypic similarities between Dlg1 knockout and reduced beta-catenin signaling.

claim: EC-specific loss of Dlg1 synergizes with genetically-directed reductions in beta-catenin signaling components.
source: EC-specific loss of Dlg1 produces a retinal vascular phenotype that closely matches the phenotype associated with reduced beta-catenin signaling, synergizes with genetically-directed reductions in beta-catenin signaling components, and can be rescued by stabilizing beta-catenin in ECs.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction experiments with Fz4, Tspan12, and Ndp shown in the manuscript.

claim: The EC-specific Dlg1 knockout phenotype can be rescued by stabilizing beta-catenin in ECs.
source: EC-specific loss of Dlg1 produces a retinal vascular phenotype that closely matches the phenotype associated with reduced beta-catenin signaling, synergizes with genetically-directed reductions in beta-catenin signaling components, and can be rescued by stabilizing beta-catenin in ECs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue with Ctnnb1flex3 allele.

claim: Transfection of Dlg1 enhances beta-catenin signaling approximately 4 fold in reporter cells with CRISPR/Cas9-mediated inactivation of Dlg1.
source: In reporter cells with CRISPR/Cas9-mediated inactivation of Dlg1, transfection of Dlg1 enhances beta-catenin signaling ~4 fold.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in STF cells.

claim: Frizzled4 contains a C-terminal PDZ-binding motif that can bind to Dlg1 PDZ domains.
source: Surprisingly, Frizzled4, which contains a C-terminal PDZ-binding motif that can bind to Dlg1 PDZ domains, appears to function independently of Dlg1 in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical binding assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: Frizzled4 appears to function independently of Dlg1 in vivo.
source: Surprisingly, Frizzled4, which contains a C-terminal PDZ-binding motif that can bind to Dlg1 PDZ domains, appears to function independently of Dlg1 in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis analyses with the Fz4MGK mutant.

claim: Proteins other than Frizzled receptors interact with Dlg1 to enhance beta-catenin signaling.
source: These data expand the repertoire of Dlg/MAGUK family functions to include a role in beta-catenin signaling, and they suggest that proteins other than Frizzled receptors interact with Dlg1 to enhance beta-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data showing Dlg1 function independent of Fz4 C-terminal binding.

claim: The mammalian retina depends on two distinct vascular networks: the choroidal and intra-retinal circulations.
source: The mammalian retina depends on two distinct vascular networks: the choroidal and intra-retinal circulations, which supply the outer third and inner two-thirds of the retina, respectively (Sun and Smith, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sun and Smith, 2018.

claim: The choroidal circulation supplies the outer third of the retina.
source: The mammalian retina depends on two distinct vascular networks: the choroidal and intra-retinal circulations, which supply the outer third and inner two-thirds of the retina, respectively (Sun and Smith, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sun and Smith, 2018.

claim: The intra-retinal circulation supplies the inner two-thirds of the retina.
source: The mammalian retina depends on two distinct vascular networks: the choroidal and intra-retinal circulations, which supply the outer third and inner two-thirds of the retina, respectively (Sun and Smith, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sun and Smith, 2018.

claim: The intra-retinal vessels originate from the optic nerve.
source: The intra-retinal vessels originate from the optic nerve and, in the first stage of their development, proliferate radially to cover the vitreal surface of the retina.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retinal vascular development.

claim: In the first stage of development, intra-retinal vessels proliferate radially to cover the vitreal surface of the retina.
source: The intra-retinal vessels originate from the optic nerve and, in the first stage of their development, proliferate radially to cover the vitreal surface of the retina.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retinal vascular development.

claim: Vessels from the superficial plexus grow into the inner retina and form two additional tiers of capillary beds – the deep and intermediate plexuses.
source: Vessels from this superficial plexus then grow into the inner retina and form two additional tiers of capillary beds – the deep and intermediate plexuses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retinal vascular development.

claim: Mature vascular endothelial cells of the CNS form a specialized diffusion barrier between blood and tissue known as the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
source: Mature vascular endothelial cells (ECs) of the central nervous system (CNS), including the retina, form a specialized diffusion barrier between blood and tissue known as the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and its retinal analog, the blood-retina barrier (BRB) (Daneman and Prat, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Daneman and Prat, 2015.

claim: The blood-retina barrier (BRB) is the retinal analog of the blood-brain barrier.
source: Mature vascular endothelial cells (ECs) of the central nervous system (CNS), including the retina, form a specialized diffusion barrier between blood and tissue known as the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and its retinal analog, the blood-retina barrier (BRB) (Daneman and Prat, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Daneman and Prat, 2015.

claim: The specialized features of CNS ECs that account for the barrier include the presence of tight junctions.
source: The specialized features of CNS ECs that account for the barrier include: (i) the presence of tight junctions; (ii) the absence of fenestrations; (iii) suppression of transcytosis; and (iv) expression of small molecule transporters and extrusion pumps.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BBB/BRB properties.

claim: The specialized features of CNS ECs that account for the barrier include the absence of fenestrations.
source: The specialized features of CNS ECs that account for the barrier include: (i) the presence of tight junctions; (ii) the absence of fenestrations; (iii) suppression of transcytosis; and (iv) expression of small molecule transporters and extrusion pumps.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BBB/BRB properties.

claim: The specialized features of CNS ECs that account for the barrier include suppression of transcytosis.
source: The specialized features of CNS ECs that account for the barrier include: (i) the presence of tight junctions; (ii) the absence of fenestrations; (iii) suppression of transcytosis; and (iv) expression of small molecule transporters and extrusion pumps.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BBB/BRB properties.

claim: The specialized features of CNS ECs that account for the barrier include expression of small molecule transporters and extrusion pumps.
source: The specialized features of CNS ECs that account for the barrier include: (i) the presence of tight junctions; (ii) the absence of fenestrations; (iii) suppression of transcytosis; and (iv) expression of small molecule transporters and extrusion pumps.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BBB/BRB properties.

claim: The BBB and BRB allow for the selective transport of small molecules across the endothelium.
source: The BBB and BRB allow for the selective transport of small molecules across the endothelium, thereby protecting the surrounding neurons and glia from toxins and other bioactive molecules.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BBB/BRB function.

claim: The BBB and BRB protect the surrounding neurons and glia from toxins and other bioactive molecules.
source: The BBB and BRB allow for the selective transport of small molecules across the endothelium, thereby protecting the surrounding neurons and glia from toxins and other bioactive molecules.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BBB/BRB function.

claim: The growth and differentiation programs of CNS ECs are controlled by beta-catenin (canonical Wnt) signaling.
source: The growth and differentiation programs of CNS ECs are controlled by multiple signaling systems, including beta-catenin (canonical Wnt) signaling (Xu et al., 2004; Stenman et al., 2008; Liebner et al., 2008; Daneman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the embryonic brain and spinal cord, neuroepithelium-derived Wnt7a and Wnt7b are the principal beta-catenin signaling ligands required for angiogenesis and BBB development.
source: In the embryonic brain and spinal cord, neuroepithelium-derived Wnt7a and Wnt7b are the principal beta-catenin signaling ligands required for angiogenesis and BBB development (Stenman et al., 2008; Daneman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stenman et al., 2008 and Daneman et al., 2009.

claim: In the adult brain, Wnt7a and Wnt7b are produced predominantly by glia.
source: In the adult brain, Wnt7a and Wnt7b are produced predominantly by glia (Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: Wnt7a and Wnt7b ligands act on ECs through a Frizzled (Fz) receptor, Lrp5/6 co-receptor, and two Wnt7a/b-specific cell-surface co-activators, Reck and Gpr124.
source: These ligands act on ECs through a Frizzled (Fz) receptor, Lrp5/6 co-receptor, and two Wnt7a/b-specific cell-surface co-activators, Reck and Gpr124 (Zhou and Nathans, 2014; Posokhova et al., 2015; Vanhollebeke et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2017; Eubelen et al., 2018; Vallon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the retina, Müller glia-derived Norrin is the predominant beta-catenin signaling ligand responsible for angiogenesis and BRB development.
source: In the retina, Müller glia-derived Norrin is the predominant beta-catenin signaling ligand responsible for angiogenesis and BRB development (Ye et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ye et al., 2009 and Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: Norrin stimulates beta-catenin signaling in retinal ECs by acting on Fz4, Lrp5, and the Norrin-specific cell-surface co-activator Tspan12.
source: Norrin stimulates beta-catenin signaling in retinal ECs by acting on Fz4, Lrp5, and the Norrin-specific cell-surface co-activator Tspan12 (Xu et al., 2004; Junge et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2004 and Junge et al., 2009.

claim: In humans, loss-of-function mutations in Norrin signaling components causes retinal hypovascularization.
source: In humans, loss-of-function mutations in each of these Norrin signaling components causes retinal hypovascularization, a phenotype that is also observed in the corresponding gene knockout mouse lines (Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018b.

claim: Retinal hypovascularization is observed in gene knockout mouse lines for Norrin signaling components.
source: In humans, loss-of-function mutations in each of these Norrin signaling components causes retinal hypovascularization, a phenotype that is also observed in the corresponding gene knockout mouse lines (Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018b.

claim: Beta-catenin signaling involves ligand-dependent receptor/co-receptor regulation of the beta-catenin destruction complex.
source: On the cytosolic side of the membrane, beta-catenin signaling involves ligand-dependent receptor/co-receptor regulation of the beta-catenin destruction complex (MacDonald et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to MacDonald et al., 2009.

claim: Dlg1 can bind to a PDZ-binding motif present at the C-terminus of several Frizzleds, including Fz4.
source: Earlier studies showed that Discs large homologue 1 [Dlg1; also called Dlgh1 or synapse-associated protein 97 (SAP97)], an intracellular scaffolding protein with PDZ and guanylate kinase domains, can bind to a PDZ-binding motif present at the C-terminus of several Frizzleds, including Fz4 (Hering and Sheng, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hering and Sheng, 2002.

claim: Dlg1 is an intracellular scaffolding protein with PDZ and guanylate kinase domains.
source: Earlier studies showed that Discs large homologue 1 [Dlg1; also called Dlgh1 or synapse-associated protein 97 (SAP97)], an intracellular scaffolding protein with PDZ and guanylate kinase domains, can bind to a PDZ-binding motif present at the C-terminus of several Frizzleds, including Fz4 (Hering and Sheng, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Dlg1 structure.

claim: Dlg1 or other Dlg family members could play a role in beta-catenin signaling via an effect on trafficking or localization of Frizzled receptors.
source: These data suggest that Dlg1 or other Dlg family members could play a role in beta-catenin signaling, presumably via an effect on trafficking or localization of Frizzled receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on prior knowledge of Dlg1-Fz4 binding.

claim: Dlg family members have been widely studied in the context of cell polarity, synaptic organization, and protein trafficking.
source: While Dlg family members have been widely studied in the context of cell polarity, synaptic organization, and protein trafficking (Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008; Walch, 2013; Won et al., 2017), their potential connection to beta-catenin signaling is largely unexplored, and, to our knowledge, is limited to only two reports, one in Drosophila that implies a stimulatory role for Dlg via stabilization of Disheveled (Liu et al., 2016) and the second in mammalian cell culture that implies an inhibitory role for Dlg1 via enhanced GSK3β phosphorylation of beta-catenin followed by ubiquitination and proteolysis (Boccitto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008; Walch, 2013; Won et al., 2017.

claim: The potential connection between Dlg family members and beta-catenin signaling is largely unexplored.
source: While Dlg family members have been widely studied in the context of cell polarity, synaptic organization, and protein trafficking (Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008; Walch, 2013; Won et al., 2017), their potential connection to beta-catenin signaling is largely unexplored, and, to our knowledge, is limited to only two reports, one in Drosophila that implies a stimulatory role for Dlg via stabilization of Disheveled (Liu et al., 2016) and the second in mammalian cell culture that implies an inhibitory role for Dlg1 via enhanced GSK3β phosphorylation of beta-catenin followed by ubiquitination and proteolysis (Boccitto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on a review of the literature.

claim: One report in Drosophila implies a stimulatory role for Dlg via stabilization of Disheveled.
source: While Dlg family members have been widely studied in the context of cell polarity, synaptic organization, and protein trafficking (Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008; Walch, 2013; Won et al., 2017), their potential connection to beta-catenin signaling is largely unexplored, and, to our knowledge, is limited to only two reports, one in Drosophila that implies a stimulatory role for Dlg via stabilization of Disheveled (Liu et al., 2016) and the second in mammalian cell culture that implies an inhibitory role for Dlg1 via enhanced GSK3β phosphorylation of beta-catenin followed by ubiquitination and proteolysis (Boccitto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: One report in mammalian cell culture implies an inhibitory role for Dlg1 via enhanced GSK3β phosphorylation of beta-catenin followed by ubiquitination and proteolysis.
source: While Dlg family members have been widely studied in the context of cell polarity, synaptic organization, and protein trafficking (Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008; Walch, 2013; Won et al., 2017), their potential connection to beta-catenin signaling is largely unexplored, and, to our knowledge, is limited to only two reports, one in Drosophila that implies a stimulatory role for Dlg via stabilization of Disheveled (Liu et al., 2016) and the second in mammalian cell culture that implies an inhibitory role for Dlg1 via enhanced GSK3β phosphorylation of beta-catenin followed by ubiquitination and proteolysis (Boccitto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boccitto et al., 2016.

claim: The mechanism of stimulation described for Drosophila Dlg involves a Disheveled-binding motif that is conserved in mammalian Dlg2 but is absent from the four other mammalian Dlg family members.
source: The mechanism of stimulation described for Drosophila Dlg involves a Disheveled-binding motif that is conserved in mammalian Dlg2 but is absent from the four other mammalian Dlg family members (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: In P7 mouse brain ECs, Dlg1 transcripts (18 FPKM) are approximately 7 fold more abundant than transcripts coding for the next most abundant family member, Dlg5 (2.5 FPKM).
source: In P7 mouse brain ECs, RNAseq shows that Dlg1 transcripts (18 FPKM) are ~7 fold more abundant than transcripts coding for the next most abundant family member, Dlg5 (2.5 FPKM); transcripts for other Dlg family members are present at even lower levels [Dlg2 (0 FPKM), Dlg3 (1.5 FPKM), and Dlg4 (1.5 FPKM)] (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Transcripts for Dlg2, Dlg3, and Dlg4 are present at lower levels than Dlg1 and Dlg5 in P7 mouse brain ECs.
source: In P7 mouse brain ECs, RNAseq shows that Dlg1 transcripts (18 FPKM) are ~7 fold more abundant than transcripts coding for the next most abundant family member, Dlg5 (2.5 FPKM); transcripts for other Dlg family members are present at even lower levels [Dlg2 (0 FPKM), Dlg3 (1.5 FPKM), and Dlg4 (1.5 FPKM)] (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Ubiquitous loss of Dlg1 leads to neonatal lethality.
source: Ubiquitous loss of Dlg1 leads to neonatal lethality (Caruana and Bernstein, 2001; Mahoney et al., 2006; Rivera et al., 2013; Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2007; Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: At P7, Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas displayed reduced density and retarded radial growth of the superficial vascular plexus relative to WT controls.
source: At P7, Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas displayed reduced density and retarded radial growth of the superficial vascular plexus relative to WT controls (Figure 1A and B; quantified in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, B, and C.

claim: At P14, the density of the superficial vascular plexus in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas appeared normal.
source: At P14, the density of the superficial vascular plexus in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas appeared normal, while the deep vascular plexus showed reduced density (Figure 1E and F; quantified in 1G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E, F, and G.

claim: At P14, the deep vascular plexus in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas showed reduced density.
source: At P14, the density of the superficial vascular plexus in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas appeared normal, while the deep vascular plexus showed reduced density (Figure 1E and F; quantified in 1G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E, F, and G.

claim: By P18, the density of the deep vascular plexus in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas had nearly caught up to the WT control.
source: By P18, the density of the deep vascular plexus in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas had nearly caught up to the WT control (Figure 1I and J; quantified in K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1I, J, and K.

claim: At all three developmental stages, a subset of ECs in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas expressed PLVAP, which was undetectable in WT controls.
source: At all three developmental stages, a subset of ECs in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas expressed the fenestral diaphragm protein plasmalemma vesicle-associated protein (PLVAP), which was undetectable in WT controls (Figure 1A and B,E and F,I and J; quantified in D, H, and L, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Retarded angiogenesis and induction of PLVAP are hallmarks of reduced beta-catenin signaling in ECs.
source: Retarded angiogenesis and induction of PLVAP are hallmarks of reduced beta-catenin signaling in ECs, as seen with loss of Fz4, Tspan12, Lrp5, or Ndp, and they correlate with the degree of reduction in beta-catenin signaling (Xia et al., 2008; Junge et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2012; Rattner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ECs in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas showed a modest reduction in the abundance of the tight junction marker Claudin5.
source: ECs in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas also showed a modest reduction in the abundance of the tight junction marker Claudin5 and a subset of ECs co-expressed Claudin5 and PLVAP, but there was no conversion of ECs from Claudin5+/PLVAP- to Claudin5-/PLVAP+, as seen in retinas with a severe decrement in EC beta-catenin signaling (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by data in the manuscript and citations to Wang et al., 2012 and Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: A subset of ECs in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas co-expressed Claudin5 and PLVAP.
source: ECs in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas also showed a modest reduction in the abundance of the tight junction marker Claudin5 and a subset of ECs co-expressed Claudin5 and PLVAP, but there was no conversion of ECs from Claudin5+/PLVAP- to Claudin5-/PLVAP+, as seen in retinas with a severe decrement in EC beta-catenin signaling (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: There was no conversion of ECs from Claudin5+/PLVAP- to Claudin5-/PLVAP+ in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas.
source: ECs in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas also showed a modest reduction in the abundance of the tight junction marker Claudin5 and a subset of ECs co-expressed Claudin5 and PLVAP, but there was no conversion of ECs from Claudin5+/PLVAP- to Claudin5-/PLVAP+, as seen in retinas with a severe decrement in EC beta-catenin signaling (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by data in the manuscript and citations to Wang et al., 2012 and Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: Heterozygous loss of Fz4 confers a near-normal vascular phenotype.
source: Since heterozygous loss of Fz4 confers a near-normal vascular phenotype (Zhou et al., 2014), we reasoned that if Dlg1 promotes beta-catenin signaling in ECs, then the combination of EC-specific loss of Dlg1 and heterozygous loss of Fz4 might produce a retinal vascular phenotype more severe than either alone.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: At P18, Dlg1fl/Δ;Fz4+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas display a dramatic reduction in vascular density specifically in the deep vascular plexus.
source: Figure 2 shows that this is the case: at P18, Dlg1fl/Δ;Fz4+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas display a dramatic reduction in vascular density specifically in the deep vascular plexus and widespread expression of PLVAP in retinal ECs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At P18, Dlg1fl/Δ;Fz4+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas display widespread expression of PLVAP in retinal ECs.
source: Figure 2 shows that this is the case: at P18, Dlg1fl/Δ;Fz4+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas display a dramatic reduction in vascular density specifically in the deep vascular plexus and widespread expression of PLVAP in retinal ECs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In Dlg1fl/Δ;Fz4+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas, the BRB was minimally impaired, as judged by the low level of sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
source: In Dlg1fl/Δ;Fz4+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas, the BRB was minimally impaired, as judged by the low level of sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Loss of Tspan12 leads to a retinal vascular phenotype that closely resembles, but is less severe than, the phenotype seen with loss of Norrin or Fz4.
source: Loss of Tspan12, a receptor co-factor for Norrin-Fz4 signaling, leads to a retinal vascular phenotype that closely resembles, but is less severe than, the phenotype seen with loss of Norrin or Fz4 (Junge et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Junge et al., 2009.

claim: Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas displayed essentially normal vascular architecture.
source: Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas (i.e. with one WT allele for each gene; Figure 3A) displayed essentially normal vascular architecture, barely detectable PLVAP expression, and no detectable sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas displayed barely detectable PLVAP expression.
source: Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas (i.e. with one WT allele for each gene; Figure 3A) displayed essentially normal vascular architecture, barely detectable PLVAP expression, and no detectable sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas displayed no detectable sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
source: Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas (i.e. with one WT allele for each gene; Figure 3A) displayed essentially normal vascular architecture, barely detectable PLVAP expression, and no detectable sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas displayed a more severe vascular phenotype compared to Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre and Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre.
source: Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas (i.e. no WT Dlg1 alleles and one WT Tspan12 allele; Figure 3B) displayed a more severe vascular phenotype compared to Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre and Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre (compare to Figures 1J and 3A, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1J, 3A, and 3B.

claim: Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas showed a greater reduction in vascular density, reduced Claudin5, increased PLVAP, and minimal sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
source: Specifically, Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12+/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas showed a greater reduction in vascular density, reduced Claudin5, increased PLVAP, and minimal sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Tspan12Δ/Δ retinas showed reduced density of the vasculature, further reductions in Claudin5, and widespread accumulation of PLVAP.
source: Tspan12Δ/Δ retinas (Figure 3C) and Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas (i.e. a single Dlg1 allele and no Tspan12 alleles; Figure 3D) showed reduced density of the vasculature, further reductions in Claudin5, and widespread accumulation of PLVAP.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas showed reduced density of the vasculature, further reductions in Claudin5, and widespread accumulation of PLVAP.
source: Tspan12Δ/Δ retinas (Figure 3C) and Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas (i.e. a single Dlg1 allele and no Tspan12 alleles; Figure 3D) showed reduced density of the vasculature, further reductions in Claudin5, and widespread accumulation of PLVAP.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both Tspan12Δ/Δ and Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre genotypes showed a moderate level of sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
source: While both genotypes showed a moderate level of sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage, leakage appears to be incrementally higher in Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage appears to be incrementally higher in Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas compared to Tspan12Δ/Δ retinas.
source: While both genotypes showed a moderate level of sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage, leakage appears to be incrementally higher in Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: The complete loss of both Dlg1 and Tspan12 (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre) produced the most severe retinal vascular phenotype, comparable to the phenotypes produced by loss of Ndp or Fz4.
source: The complete loss of both Dlg1 and Tspan12 (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre; Figure 3E) produced the most severe retinal vascular phenotype, comparable to the phenotypes produced by loss of Ndp or Fz4, with nearly complete conversion of veins and capillaries from Claudin5+/PLVAP- to Claudin5-/PLVAP+ and severe sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas showed nearly complete conversion of veins and capillaries from Claudin5+/PLVAP- to Claudin5-/PLVAP+.
source: The complete loss of both Dlg1 and Tspan12 (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre; Figure 3E) produced the most severe retinal vascular phenotype, comparable to the phenotypes produced by loss of Ndp or Fz4, with nearly complete conversion of veins and capillaries from Claudin5+/PLVAP- to Claudin5-/PLVAP+ and severe sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas showed severe sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
source: The complete loss of both Dlg1 and Tspan12 (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre; Figure 3E) produced the most severe retinal vascular phenotype, comparable to the phenotypes produced by loss of Ndp or Fz4, with nearly complete conversion of veins and capillaries from Claudin5+/PLVAP- to Claudin5-/PLVAP+ and severe sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Arteries do not convert to a PLVAP+ state with loss of beta-catenin signaling.
source: As described previously, arteries do not convert to a PLVAP+ state with loss of beta-catenin signaling (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2012.

claim: The variable increase in vascular density in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas reflects the hypertrophy of vascular glomeruloids.
source: The variable increase in vascular density in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas (quantified in Figure 3F) reflects the hypertrophy of vascular glomeruloids, a secondary response to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) secreted by the severely hypoxic retina and a hallmark of Ndp and Fz4 mutant retinas (Ye et al., 2009; Rattner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3F and citations to Ye et al., 2009 and Rattner et al., 2014.

claim: Hypertrophy of vascular glomeruloids is a secondary response to VEGF secreted by the severely hypoxic retina.
source: The variable increase in vascular density in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas (quantified in Figure 3F) reflects the hypertrophy of vascular glomeruloids, a secondary response to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) secreted by the severely hypoxic retina and a hallmark of Ndp and Fz4 mutant retinas (Ye et al., 2009; Rattner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ye et al., 2009 and Rattner et al., 2014.

claim: Vascular glomeruloids are a hallmark of Ndp and Fz4 mutant retinas.
source: The variable increase in vascular density in Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas (quantified in Figure 3F) reflects the hypertrophy of vascular glomeruloids, a secondary response to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) secreted by the severely hypoxic retina and a hallmark of Ndp and Fz4 mutant retinas (Ye et al., 2009; Rattner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ye et al., 2009 and Rattner et al., 2014.

claim: Beta-catenin signaling in brain ECs depends on the partially redundant Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck and Norrin/Fz4/Tspan12 signaling systems.
source: As noted in the Introduction, beta-catenin signaling in brain ECs depends on the partially redundant Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck and Norrin/Fz4/Tspan12 signaling systems and is required for the development and maintenance of the BBB (Wang et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou and Nathans, 2014; Cho et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Beta-catenin signaling is required for the development and maintenance of the BBB.
source: As noted in the Introduction, beta-catenin signaling in brain ECs depends on the partially redundant Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck and Norrin/Fz4/Tspan12 signaling systems and is required for the development and maintenance of the BBB (Wang et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou and Nathans, 2014; Cho et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Genetic loss of beta-catenin signaling components compromises the BBB in a graded and region-specific fashion.
source: Genetic loss of these signaling components compromises the BBB in a graded and region-specific fashion, with progressive decrements in beta-catenin signaling producing progressively more severe defects in BBB integrity (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018a; Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou and Nathans, 2014; Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Progressive decrements in beta-catenin signaling produce progressively more severe defects in BBB integrity.
source: Genetic loss of these signaling components compromises the BBB in a graded and region-specific fashion, with progressive decrements in beta-catenin signaling producing progressively more severe defects in BBB integrity (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018a; Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou and Nathans, 2014; Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ndp null mice have mild BBB defects, primarily in the cerebellum and olfactory bulb.
source: For example, Ndp null mice have mild BBB defects, primarily in the cerebellum and olfactory bulb, while Tspan12 null mice have no BBB defects, consistent with the more modest effect of Tspan12 on Norrin/Fz4/Tspan12 signaling (Junge et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Junge et al., 2009 and Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: Tspan12 null mice have no BBB defects.
source: For example, Ndp null mice have mild BBB defects, primarily in the cerebellum and olfactory bulb, while Tspan12 null mice have no BBB defects, consistent with the more modest effect of Tspan12 on Norrin/Fz4/Tspan12 signaling (Junge et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Junge et al., 2009 and Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: In the cerebellum, signaling by the Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck system is apparently sufficient to compensate for the loss of Tspan12.
source: In the cerebellum, signaling by the Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck system is apparently sufficient to compensate for the loss of Tspan12, but it does not fully compensate for the loss of Ndp (Zhou et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: In the cerebellum, signaling by the Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck system does not fully compensate for the loss of Ndp.
source: In the cerebellum, signaling by the Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck system is apparently sufficient to compensate for the loss of Tspan12, but it does not fully compensate for the loss of Ndp (Zhou et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: The vasculature in the cerebellum is especially sensitive to the level of endothelial beta-catenin signaling.
source: Since previous work has shown that the vasculature in the cerebellum is especially sensitive to the level of endothelial beta-catenin signaling (Zhou et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018a), we have visualized cerebellar sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage and quantified cerebellar EC expression of PLVAP and the glucose transporter GLUT1, a marker of BBB-competent ECs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: GLUT1 is a marker of BBB-competent ECs.
source: Since previous work has shown that the vasculature in the cerebellum is especially sensitive to the level of endothelial beta-catenin signaling (Zhou et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018a), we have visualized cerebellar sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage and quantified cerebellar EC expression of PLVAP and the glucose transporter GLUT1, a marker of BBB-competent ECs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about GLUT1.

claim: Halving the dose of endothelial Dlg1 (Dlg1fl/+;Tie2-Cre) produced no loss of GLUT1 expression, no increase in PLVAP expression, and no BBB breakdown.
source: Halving the dose of endothelial Dlg1 (Dlg1fl/+;Tie2-Cre), eliminating endothelial Dlg1 (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre), or halving the dosage of endothelial Dlg1 on the background of a Tspan12 knockout (Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre) produced no loss of GLUT1 expression, no increase in PLVAP expression, and no BBB breakdown as assessed by sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4A.

claim: Eliminating endothelial Dlg1 (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre) produced no loss of GLUT1 expression, no increase in PLVAP expression, and no BBB breakdown.
source: Halving the dose of endothelial Dlg1 (Dlg1fl/+;Tie2-Cre), eliminating endothelial Dlg1 (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre), or halving the dosage of endothelial Dlg1 on the background of a Tspan12 knockout (Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre) produced no loss of GLUT1 expression, no increase in PLVAP expression, and no BBB breakdown as assessed by sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Halving the dosage of endothelial Dlg1 on the background of a Tspan12 knockout (Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre) produced no loss of GLUT1 expression, no increase in PLVAP expression, and no BBB breakdown.
source: Halving the dose of endothelial Dlg1 (Dlg1fl/+;Tie2-Cre), eliminating endothelial Dlg1 (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre), or halving the dosage of endothelial Dlg1 on the background of a Tspan12 knockout (Dlg1fl/+;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre) produced no loss of GLUT1 expression, no increase in PLVAP expression, and no BBB breakdown as assessed by sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A complete loss of endothelial Dlg1 on the background of a Tspan12 knockout (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre) partially compromises the cerebellar BBB.
source: However, a complete loss of endothelial Dlg1 on the background of a Tspan12 knockout (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre) partially compromises the cerebellar BBB, as seen by a small decrease in the fraction of GLUT1+ ECs, an increase in the fraction of PLVAP+ ECs, and localized sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre brains show a small decrease in the fraction of GLUT1+ ECs.
source: However, a complete loss of endothelial Dlg1 on the background of a Tspan12 knockout (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre) partially compromises the cerebellar BBB, as seen by a small decrease in the fraction of GLUT1+ ECs, an increase in the fraction of PLVAP+ ECs, and localized sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre brains show an increase in the fraction of PLVAP+ ECs.
source: However, a complete loss of endothelial Dlg1 on the background of a Tspan12 knockout (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre) partially compromises the cerebellar BBB, as seen by a small decrease in the fraction of GLUT1+ ECs, an increase in the fraction of PLVAP+ ECs, and localized sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre brains show localized sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
source: However, a complete loss of endothelial Dlg1 on the background of a Tspan12 knockout (Dlg1fl/Δ;Tspan12Δ/Δ;Tie2-Cre) partially compromises the cerebellar BBB, as seen by a small decrease in the fraction of GLUT1+ ECs, an increase in the fraction of PLVAP+ ECs, and localized sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A comparison of Dlg1fl/+;NdpΔ/Y;Tie2-Cre vs. Dlg1fl/Δ;NdpΔ/Y;Tie2-Cre shows a dramatic worsening of BBB breakdown in both the cerebellum and hindbrain with loss of both Dlg1 alleles.
source: Similarly, a comparison of heterozygous loss of Dlg1 on the background of a Ndp knockout (Dlg1fl/+;NdpΔ/Y;Tie2-Cre) vs. homozygous loss of Dlg1 on the background of a Ndp knockout (Dlg1fl/Δ;NdpΔ/Y;Tie2-Cre) shows a dramatic worsening of BBB breakdown in both the cerebellum and hindbrain with loss of both Dlg1 alleles (compare Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The severe Dlg1fl/Δ;NdpΔ/Y;Tie2-Cre phenotype closely resembles the phenotypes observed when both Norrin/Fz4 and Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck signaling are compromised.
source: The severe Dlg1fl/Δ;NdpΔ/Y;Tie2-Cre phenotype closely resembles the phenotypes observed when both Norrin/Fz4 and Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck signaling are compromised (Zhou et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: The greater BBB breakdown in Dlg1fl/Δ;NdpΔ/Y;Tie2-Cre brains compared to Dlg1fl/+;NdpΔ/Y;Tie2-Cre brains indicates that Dlg1 function is not limited to the Norrin/Fz4/Tspan12 signaling pathway.
source: We note that the greater BBB breakdown in Dlg1fl/Δ;NdpΔ/Y;Tie2-Cre brains compared to Dlg1fl/+;NdpΔ/Y;Tie2-Cre brains indicates that Dlg1 function is not limited to the Norrin/Fz4/Tspan12 signaling pathway, which is eliminated with loss of Ndp.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data comparing different genotypes.

claim: The simplest explanation for the genetic interactions is that Dlg1 normally promotes both Norrin/Fz4/Tspan12 signaling and Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck signaling.
source: The simplest explanation for the genetic interactions shown in Figures 2–4 is that Dlg1 normally promotes both Norrin/Fz4/Tspan12 signaling and Wnt7/Fz/Gpr124/Reck signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data.

claim: Constitutive EC-specific activation of beta-catenin signaling, as produced by Ctnnb1flex3/+;Tie2-Cre, is lethal during embryonic development.
source: For this experiment, recombination was induced with CreER and 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4HT) treatment in the immediate postnatal period because constitutive EC-specific activation of beta-catenin signaling, as produced by Ctnnb1flex3/+;Tie2-Cre, is lethal during embryonic development.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: At P7, Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2Cre retinas show increased PLVAP accumulation and sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage at the leading edge of the plexus.
source: At this age, the Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2Cre retinal vasculature also shows increased PLVAP accumulation and sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage at the leading edge of the plexus (Figure 1B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; quantified in Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Figure 1D.

claim: Dlg1fl/Δ;Pdgfb-CreER mice treated with 4HT at P0 and P1 showed reduced vascular density, increased PLVAP levels, and extensive sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage when compared to 4HT-treated control mice.
source: Consistent with the Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2Cre phenotype, Dlg1fl/Δ;Pdgfb-CreER mice that were treated with 4HT at P0 and P1 showed reduced vascular density, increased PLVAP levels, and extensive sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage when compared to 4HT-treated control mice (Dlg1fl/Δ) (Figure 5A–C; quantified in Figures 5E, G and H; two examples of Dlg1fl/Δ;Pdgfb-CreER retinas are shown to show the consistency of the phenotype).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5A-C, E, G, and H.

claim: The retinal vascular defects in Dlg1fl/Δ;Pdgfb-CreER mice were almost completely reversed upon EC-specific stabilization of beta-catenin (Dlg1fl/Δ; Ctnnb1flex3/+;Pdgfb-CreER).
source: Strikingly, the retinal vascular defects in Dlg1fl/Δ;Pdgfb-CreER mice were almost completely reversed upon EC-specific stabilization of beta-catenin (Dlg1fl/Δ; Ctnnb1flex3/+;Pdgfb-CreER), as seen in Figure 5D and quantified in Figure 5E–H.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5D-H.

claim: Over-production of Dlg1 enhances beta-catenin signaling in STF cells in the presence of Norrin and Fz4.
source: To further assess the role of Dlg1 in beta-catenin signaling, we began by asking whether over-production of Dlg1 enhances signaling in a Super TOP Flash (STF) luciferase reporter cell line in the presence of Norrin and Fz4, which together produce a 20-50x induction of luciferase over background (Xu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in STF cells.

claim: Norrin and Fz4 together produce a 20-50x induction of luciferase over background in STF cells.
source: To further assess the role of Dlg1 in beta-catenin signaling, we began by asking whether over-production of Dlg1 enhances signaling in a Super TOP Flash (STF) luciferase reporter cell line in the presence of Norrin and Fz4, which together produce a 20-50x induction of luciferase over background (Xu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2004.

claim: Myc-Dlg1 transfection produces a bell-shaped curve of signal strength vs. plasmid concentration, with an optimal dose at 2.5 ng/well and a maximum stimulation of approximately 2 fold in WT STF cells.
source: Figure 6A shows a bell-shaped curve of signal strength vs. N-terminal Myc-epitope-tagged Dlg1 (Myc-Dlg1) plasmid concentration, with an optimal dose at 2.5 ng/well and a maximum stimulation of ~2 fold.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: STF cells have substantial levels of transcripts coding for Dlg1 (14 FPKM), Dlg3 (20 FPKM), and Dlg5 (7.4 FPKM).
source: Consistent with this idea, RNAseq shows that STF cells have substantial levels of transcripts coding for Dlg1 (14 FPKM), Dlg3 (20 FPKM), and the divergent family member Dlg5 (7.4 FPKM), with lower levels of transcripts coding for Dlg2 (0.1 FPKM) and Dlg4 (0.8 FPKM).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data.

claim: STF cells have lower levels of transcripts coding for Dlg2 (0.1 FPKM) and Dlg4 (0.8 FPKM).
source: Consistent with this idea, RNAseq shows that STF cells have substantial levels of transcripts coding for Dlg1 (14 FPKM), Dlg3 (20 FPKM), and the divergent family member Dlg5 (7.4 FPKM), with lower levels of transcripts coding for Dlg2 (0.1 FPKM) and Dlg4 (0.8 FPKM).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data.

claim: Transfection of Dlg1 knockout STF cells with Norrin and Fz4, together with Myc-Dlg1, showed a lower baseline level of beta-catenin signaling without transfected Dlg1.
source: Transfection of both knockout cell lines with Norrin and Fz4, together with Myc-Dlg1, showed (i) a lower baseline level of beta-catenin signaling without transfected Dlg1 and (ii) a dose response curve similar to the one obtained with the parental STF line, except that the optimal Myc-Dlg1 plasmid concentration was increased ~1.5 fold and the maximal fold stimulation increased from ~2 fold to ~4 fold (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: In Dlg1 knockout STF cells, the optimal Myc-Dlg1 plasmid concentration was increased approximately 1.5 fold compared to parental STF cells.
source: Transfection of both knockout cell lines with Norrin and Fz4, together with Myc-Dlg1, showed (i) a lower baseline level of beta-catenin signaling without transfected Dlg1 and (ii) a dose response curve similar to the one obtained with the parental STF line, except that the optimal Myc-Dlg1 plasmid concentration was increased ~1.5 fold and the maximal fold stimulation increased from ~2 fold to ~4 fold (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: In Dlg1 knockout STF cells, the maximal fold stimulation increased from approximately 2 fold to approximately 4 fold.
source: Transfection of both knockout cell lines with Norrin and Fz4, together with Myc-Dlg1, showed (i) a lower baseline level of beta-catenin signaling without transfected Dlg1 and (ii) a dose response curve similar to the one obtained with the parental STF line, except that the optimal Myc-Dlg1 plasmid concentration was increased ~1.5 fold and the maximal fold stimulation increased from ~2 fold to ~4 fold (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Co-expressed Myc-Dlg1 produced a 3- to 4-fold increase in luciferase activity for the majority of Wnt ligands in Dlg1 KO STF cells.
source: We observed a 3- to 4-fold increase in luciferase activity for the majority of Wnt ligands upon co-transfection with Myc-Dlg1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Co-expressed Myc-Dlg1 had little effect on signaling by Wnt7a and Wnt7b.
source: Interestingly, co-expressed Myc-Dlg1 had little effect on signaling by Wnt7a and Wnt7b (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Myc-Dlg1 co-transfection of Dlg1 KO STF cells transfected with Wnt7a, Gpr124, and Reck increased beta-catenin signaling by only approximately 1.5 fold at the optimal Myc-Dlg1 plasmid concentration of 2.5 ng/well.
source: Although the C-terminus of Gpr124 contains a conserved PDZ-binding domain that has been reported to directly interact with Dlg1 (Yamamoto et al., 2004; Posokhova et al., 2015), Myc-Dlg1 co-transfection of Dlg1 KO STF cells transfected with Wnt7a, Gpr124, and Reck increased beta-catenin signaling by only ~1.5 fold at the optimal Myc-Dlg1 plasmid concentration of 2.5 ng/well (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The C-terminus of Gpr124 contains a conserved PDZ-binding domain that has been reported to directly interact with Dlg1.
source: Although the C-terminus of Gpr124 contains a conserved PDZ-binding domain that has been reported to directly interact with Dlg1 (Yamamoto et al., 2004; Posokhova et al., 2015), Myc-Dlg1 co-transfection of Dlg1 KO STF cells transfected with Wnt7a, Gpr124, and Reck increased beta-catenin signaling by only ~1.5 fold at the optimal Myc-Dlg1 plasmid concentration of 2.5 ng/well (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamamoto et al., 2004 and Posokhova et al., 2015.

claim: Robust stimulation of beta-catenin signaling was produced by Myc-Dlg1, Myc-Dlg2, and Myc-Dlg4 in Dlg1 KO STF cells transfected with Norrin and Fz4.
source: In Dlg1 KO STF cells transfected with Norrin, Fz4, and the individual Dlg family members, robust stimulation of beta-catenin signaling was produced by Myc-Dlg1, Myc-Dlg2, and Myc-Dlg4, with a bell-shaped (Dlg1) or monotonic (Dlg2 and Dlg4) plasmid concentration dependence (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Myc-Dlg3 and V5-Dlg5 produced minimal stimulation of beta-catenin signaling in Dlg1 KO STF cells transfected with Norrin and Fz4.
source: In contrast, Myc-Dlg3 and V5-Dlg5 produced minimal stimulation (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Dlg2 and Dlg4 are the Dlg family members most capable of substituting for Dlg1.
source: These data imply that Dlg2 and Dlg4 are the Dlg family members most capable of substituting for Dlg1.
evidence: This is inferred from the luciferase assay data.

claim: In both CNS ECs and STF cells, where Dlg2 and Dlg4 transcripts are relatively rare, Dlg1 is likely to be the most important family member for beta-catenin signaling.
source: Thus, in both CNS ECs and STF cells, where Dlg2 and Dlg4 transcripts are relatively rare, Dlg1 is likely to be the most important family member for beta-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression data and functional assays.

claim: A previous study reported that a C-terminal peptide from Fz4, which ends with the consensus PDZ-binding motif ETVV, can interact directly with a fragment of Dlg1 comprising PDZ domains 1 and 2.
source: Using the yeast two-hybrid system, a previous study reported that a C-terminal peptide from Fz4, which ends with the consensus PDZ-binding motif ETVV [conforming to the type I C-terminal PDZ-binding motif consensus S/T-X-V/L (Bezprozvanny and Maximov, 2001), can interact directly with a fragment of Dlg1 comprising PDZ domains 1 and 2 (Hering and Sheng, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hering and Sheng, 2002.

claim: Myc-Dlg1 binds to the wild type version of Rim-Fz4 but not to a mutant version in which the four carboxyl-terminal residues were changed from ETVV to AAAA.
source: In HEK/293T cells that were transiently co-transfected with Rim-Fz4 and Myc-Dlg1, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) with anti-Myc or anti-Rim antibodies showed that Myc-Dlg1 binds to the wild type (WT) version of Rim-Fz4 but not to a mutant version in which the four carboxyl-terminal residues were changed from ETVV to AAAA (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Dlg1 binding to Fz4 requires the Fz4 PDZ-binding motif.
source: This experiment confirms that Dlg1 binding requires the Fz4 PDZ-binding motif.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data.

claim: With anti-Myc pull-down, co-IP efficiency is variably reduced for ΔPDZ1, substantially reduced for ΔPDZ2, and unaffected for ΔPDZ3.
source: Transient co-transfection of Rim-Fz4 with WT, ΔPDZ1, ΔPDZ2, or ΔPDZ3 versions of Myc-Dlg1 showed that: (i) with anti-Myc pull-down, co-IP efficiency is variably reduced for ΔPDZ1, substantially reduced for ΔPDZ2, and unaffected for ΔPDZ3, and (ii) with anti-Rim pull-down, co-IP efficiency is substantially reduced for both ΔPDZ1 and ΔPDZ2, and unaffected for ΔPDZ3 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: With anti-Rim pull-down, co-IP efficiency is substantially reduced for both ΔPDZ1 and ΔPDZ2, and unaffected for ΔPDZ3.
source: Transient co-transfection of Rim-Fz4 with WT, ΔPDZ1, ΔPDZ2, or ΔPDZ3 versions of Myc-Dlg1 showed that: (i) with anti-Myc pull-down, co-IP efficiency is variably reduced for ΔPDZ1, substantially reduced for ΔPDZ2, and unaffected for ΔPDZ3, and (ii) with anti-Rim pull-down, co-IP efficiency is substantially reduced for both ΔPDZ1 and ΔPDZ2, and unaffected for ΔPDZ3 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: ΔPDZ1 and ΔPDZ2 had greatly reduced peptide binding to the Fz4 C-terminal peptide compared to WT Dlg1.
source: This experiment shows that, compared to WT Dlg1, ΔPDZ1 and ΔPDZ2 had greatly reduced peptide binding and ΔPDZ3 had modestly reduced peptide binding.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: ΔPDZ3 had modestly reduced peptide binding to the Fz4 C-terminal peptide compared to WT Dlg1.
source: This experiment shows that, compared to WT Dlg1, ΔPDZ1 and ΔPDZ2 had greatly reduced peptide binding and ΔPDZ3 had modestly reduced peptide binding.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: ΔPDZ2+3 had greatly reduced binding to the Fz4 C-terminal peptide.
source: Using the same assay, ΔPDZ2+3 (i.e. simultaneous deletion of domains 2 and 3) had greatly reduced binding, and ΔPDZ1+2 and ΔPDZ1+2+3 had little or no binding (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: ΔPDZ1+2 and ΔPDZ1+2+3 had little or no binding to the Fz4 C-terminal peptide.
source: Using the same assay, ΔPDZ2+3 (i.e. simultaneous deletion of domains 2 and 3) had greatly reduced binding, and ΔPDZ1+2 and ΔPDZ1+2+3 had little or no binding (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: MBP-PDZ1+2 showed efficient and specific peptide capture of the Fz4 C-terminal peptide.
source: This experiment showed efficient and specific peptide capture of MBP-PDZ1+2, but not of MBP-PDZ1 or MBP-PDZ2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: MBP-PDZ1 and MBP-PDZ2 did not show efficient peptide capture of the Fz4 C-terminal peptide.
source: This experiment showed efficient and specific peptide capture of MBP-PDZ1+2, but not of MBP-PDZ1 or MBP-PDZ2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Dlg1 over-expression has no effect on total or surface accumulation of Fz4.
source: By immunoblotting of Rim-Fz4 following surface biotinylation, we observed no effect of Dlg1 over-expression on total or surface accumulation of Fz4.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The total abundance of Tspan12 was unaltered by Dlg1 over-expression.
source: In a parallel experiment with Tspan12, the total abundance of Tspan12 was unaltered by Dlg1 over-expression and cell surface Tspan12 was below the limit of detection either with or without Dlg1.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell surface Tspan12 was below the limit of detection either with or without Dlg1.
source: In a parallel experiment with Tspan12, the total abundance of Tspan12 was unaltered by Dlg1 over-expression and cell surface Tspan12 was below the limit of detection either with or without Dlg1.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dlg1 does not enhance Fz4 trafficking to the plasma membrane.
source: These data indicate that Dlg1, while capable of interacting with the Fz4 C-terminus, does not enhance Fz4 trafficking to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the surface biotinylation data.

claim: For the Dlg1-Fz4 interaction, the relative importance of the Dlg1 PDZ domains is PDZ2 >PDZ1>>PDZ3.
source: In summary, using multiple approaches, we confirm specific binding between the PDZ domains of Dlg1 and the C-terminus of Fz4. For this interaction, the relative importance of the Dlg1 PDZ domains is PDZ2 >PDZ1>>PDZ3.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding assay data.

claim: Deletion of L27+PEST, PDZ1, PDZ2, or PDZ1+2 domains reduced Dlg1 activity by approximately 25% in STF cells.
source: For example, deletion of L27+PEST (mutant #1), PDZ1 (mutant #2), PDZ2 (mutant #3), or PDZ1+2 (mutant #5) domains reduced Dlg1 activity by ~25%.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All of the mutants that include a deletion of PDZ3 reduced Dlg1 activity by approximately 30–50% in STF cells.
source: All of the mutants that include a deletion of PDZ3 (mutant #4, #6, and #7) reduced activity by ~30–50%.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The greatest loss of Dlg1 function was observed upon deletion of the C-terminal SH3+Hook+guanylate kinase (GUK) domains.
source: The greatest loss of function was observed upon deletion of the C-terminal SH3+Hook+guanylate kinase (GUK) domains (mutant #11), with modest decreases upon deletion of either SH3+Hook (mutant #8) or Hook+GUK (mutant #10).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Multiple domains within Dlg1 contribute to its activity in beta-catenin signaling.
source: These data imply that multiple domains within Dlg1 contribute to its activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the domain deletion data.

claim: Fz4(4A) elicited a approximately 5 fold lower response than WT Fz4 in Dlg1 KO STF cells.
source: A comparison of the luciferase response of Dlg1 KO STF cells to transfection with Norrin and WT Fz4 vs. Fz4(4A), together with variable amounts of Myc-Dlg1 plasmid, showed that Fz4(4A) elicited a ~5 fold lower response than WT Fz4 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D), roughly consistent with the several-fold lower level of Fz4(4A) accumulation, as determined by immunoblotting (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D and Figure 8C.

claim: The combination of Norrin and Fz4(4A) exhibited a similar Myc-Dlg1 dose dependence as did the combination of Norrin and WT Fz4.
source: Importantly, the combination of Norrin and Fz4(4A) exhibited a similar Myc-Dlg1 dose dependence – especially at low Myc-Dlg1 plasmid concentrations – as did the combination of Norrin and WT Fz4, suggesting that Dlg1 stimulates beta-catenin signaling in the same manner in these two contexts.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The Dlg1-dependent stimulation of beta-catenin signaling activity by a Fz4 mutant that abrogates Dlg1-Fz4 binding argues that this interaction is dispensable for beta-catenin signaling in STF reporter cells.
source: In conclusion, the Dlg1-dependent stimulation of beta-catenin signaling activity by a Fz4 mutant that abrogates Dlg1-Fz4 binding argues that this interaction is dispensable for beta-catenin signaling, at least in STF reporter cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the luciferase assay data with Fz4(4A).

claim: The TVV-to-MGK substitution in Fz4 eliminates binding to Myc-Dlg1.
source: As would be predicted based on structure-function analyses of the interaction between PDZ-binding motifs and the Dlg1 PDZ domains (Zhang et al., 2011; Slep, 2012), the TVV-to-MGK substitution eliminates binding to Myc-Dlg1, as determined by the biotin-peptide binding assay (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B and citations to Zhang et al., 2011 and Slep, 2012.

claim: Fz4(MGK) accumulates in transfected HEK/293T cells to a level that is several-fold lower than WT Fz4.
source: We also observed that Fz4(MGK), like Fz4(4A), accumulates in transfected HEK/293T cells to a level that is several-fold lower than WT Fz4 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: At P18, Fz4MGK/MGK mice have normal retinal vascular architecture and density.
source: At P18, Fz4MGK/MGK mice have normal retinal vascular architecture and density, retinal ECs are uniformly Claudin5+/PLVAP-, and the BRB is intact as judged by the absence of sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 8D; quantified in 8G-I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 8D and 8G-I.

claim: At P18, retinal ECs in Fz4MGK/MGK mice are uniformly Claudin5+/PLVAP-.
source: At P18, Fz4MGK/MGK mice have normal retinal vascular architecture and density, retinal ECs are uniformly Claudin5+/PLVAP-, and the BRB is intact as judged by the absence of sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 8D; quantified in 8G-I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 8D and 8G-I.

claim: At P18, the BRB is intact in Fz4MGK/MGK mice as judged by the absence of sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
source: At P18, Fz4MGK/MGK mice have normal retinal vascular architecture and density, retinal ECs are uniformly Claudin5+/PLVAP-, and the BRB is intact as judged by the absence of sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 8D; quantified in 8G-I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 8D and 8G-I.

claim: Fz4MGK/MGK mice have normal brain vascular architecture and barrier integrity.
source: Fz4MGK/MGK mice also have normal brain vascular architecture and barrier integrity.
evidence: This is stated based on observations from the experiments.

claim: Homozygosity for a Fz4 null allele produces a severe retinal vascular phenotype.
source: Since homozygosity for a Fz4 null allele produces a severe retinal vascular phenotype and loss of BBB integrity in the cerebellum and olfactory bulb, these data imply that the Fz4MGK protein possesses substantial function in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Homozygosity for a Fz4 null allele produces loss of BBB integrity in the cerebellum and olfactory bulb.
source: Since homozygosity for a Fz4 null allele produces a severe retinal vascular phenotype and loss of BBB integrity in the cerebellum and olfactory bulb, these data imply that the Fz4MGK protein possesses substantial function in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: The Fz4MGK protein possesses substantial function in vivo.
source: Since homozygosity for a Fz4 null allele produces a severe retinal vascular phenotype and loss of BBB integrity in the cerebellum and olfactory bulb, these data imply that the Fz4MGK protein possesses substantial function in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Fz4MGK/MGK and Fz4 null phenotypes.

claim: At P18, Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas show mildly elevated PLVAP expression in ECs and mild sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
source: Contrary to the first of these predictions, at P18 Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas show mildly elevated PLVAP expression in ECs and mild sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 8E; quantified in 8G-I; see also Figure 1J–L), neither of which are present in Fz4MGK/MGK retinas.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 8E, 8G-I, and 1J-L.

claim: Fz4MGK/MGK;Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas show reduced vascular density, decreased Claudin5 and increased PLVAP in ECs, and widespread sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
source: Contrary to the second of these predictions, Fz4MGK/MGK;Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas show reduced vascular density, decreased Claudin5 and increased PLVAP in ECs, and widespread sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 8F–I) – phenotypes that are more severe than those of Fz4MGK/MGK or Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 8F-I.

claim: The phenotypes of Fz4MGK/MGK;Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas are more severe than those of Fz4MGK/MGK or Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas.
source: Contrary to the second of these predictions, Fz4MGK/MGK;Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas show reduced vascular density, decreased Claudin5 and increased PLVAP in ECs, and widespread sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage (Figure 8F–I) – phenotypes that are more severe than those of Fz4MGK/MGK or Dlg1fl/Δ;Tie2-Cre retinas.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 8F-I.

claim: Dlg1 activates beta-catenin signaling and controls retinal angiogenesis and BRB development and maintenance by a mechanism that is independent of its interaction with the C-terminus of Fz4.
source: These findings imply that Dlg1 activates beta-catenin signaling and controls retinal angiogenesis and BRB development and maintenance by a mechanism that is independent of its interaction with the C-terminus of Fz4.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data with Fz4MGK.

claim: The first Dlg family member was identified in Drosophila where its loss-of-function phenotype causes neoplastic transformation of imaginal disc cells.
source: The first Dlg family member was identified in Drosophila where its loss-of-function phenotype causes neoplastic transformation of imaginal disc cells (Woods and Bryant, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Woods and Bryant, 1991.

claim: In vertebrate epithelial cells, Dlg1 localizes to the basolateral membrane.
source: In vertebrate epithelial cells, Dlg1 localizes to the basolateral membrane, but its role in epithelial polarity is less clear, as Dlg1 knockout mice show no obvious epithelial polarity defects (Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2007; Mahoney et al., 2006), a result that could reflect redundancy with one or more of the four other mammalian Dlg family members (Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2007; Mahoney et al., 2006; and Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008.

claim: Dlg1 knockout mice show no obvious epithelial polarity defects.
source: In vertebrate epithelial cells, Dlg1 localizes to the basolateral membrane, but its role in epithelial polarity is less clear, as Dlg1 knockout mice show no obvious epithelial polarity defects (Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2007; Mahoney et al., 2006), a result that could reflect redundancy with one or more of the four other mammalian Dlg family members (Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2007 and Mahoney et al., 2006.

claim: The lack of epithelial polarity defects in Dlg1 knockout mice could reflect redundancy with one or more of the four other mammalian Dlg family members.
source: In vertebrate epithelial cells, Dlg1 localizes to the basolateral membrane, but its role in epithelial polarity is less clear, as Dlg1 knockout mice show no obvious epithelial polarity defects (Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2007; Mahoney et al., 2006), a result that could reflect redundancy with one or more of the four other mammalian Dlg family members (Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008.

claim: In neurons, Dlg1, Dlg2, Dlg3, and Dlg4 control receptor and channel localization and trafficking.
source: The best understood role for mammalian Dlg family members is in neurons, where Dlg1 (SAP-97), Dlg2 (PSD-93/Chapsyn-110), Dlg3 (SAP-102), and Dlg4 (PSD-95/SAP-90) control receptor and channel localization and trafficking, and loss or over-expression of Dlg family members alters synaptic transmission and/or synaptic plasticity (Xu, 2011; Fourie et al., 2014; Won et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu, 2011; Fourie et al., 2014; Won et al., 2017.

claim: Loss or over-expression of Dlg family members alters synaptic transmission and/or synaptic plasticity.
source: The best understood role for mammalian Dlg family members is in neurons, where Dlg1 (SAP-97), Dlg2 (PSD-93/Chapsyn-110), Dlg3 (SAP-102), and Dlg4 (PSD-95/SAP-90) control receptor and channel localization and trafficking, and loss or over-expression of Dlg family members alters synaptic transmission and/or synaptic plasticity (Xu, 2011; Fourie et al., 2014; Won et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu, 2011; Fourie et al., 2014; Won et al., 2017.

claim: In the adult mouse brain, Dlg proteins are expressed in astrocytes, neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ECs.
source: In the adult mouse brain, Dlg proteins are expressed in astrocytes, neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ECs (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Accumulating evidence implicates Dlg1 and other Dlg family members in protein trafficking and localization in non-neuronal contexts.
source: In addition to their roles in neurons, accumulating evidence implicates Dlg1 and other Dlg family members in protein trafficking and localization in non-neuronal contexts (Walch, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Walch, 2013.

claim: APC has a C-terminal PDZ-binding motif that binds to the PDZ1 and PDZ2 domains of Dlg1 with affinities of 18 uM and 1 uM, respectively.
source: One obvious candidate for interacting with Dlg1 in the context of beta-catenin signaling is the Adenomatous Polyposis Coli (APC) protein, which has a C-terminal PDZ-binding motif that binds to the PDZ1 and PDZ2 domains of Dlg1 with affinities of 18 uM and 1 uM, respectively (Zhang et al., 2011; Sotelo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2011 and Sotelo et al., 2012.

claim: The atomic resolution structures of the APC peptide-Dlg1 PDZ1 and PDZ2 complexes show the canonical mode of binding.
source: The corresponding atomic resolution structures of these two peptide-PDZ complexes show the canonical mode of binding (Zhang et al., 2011; Slep, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2011 and Slep, 2012.

claim: APC is a large (~300 kDa) protein that plays an important role in assembling the beta-catenin destruction complex.
source: APC is a large (~300 kDa) protein that plays an important role in assembling the beta-catenin destruction complex (Munemitsu et al., 1995; Rubinfeld et al., 1996; Stamos and Weis, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Munemitsu et al., 1995; Rubinfeld et al., 1996; Stamos and Weis, 2013.

claim: APC binding partners include the kinesin KAP3.
source: In addition to binding to Dlg1, APC binding partners include the kinesin KAP3 (Jimbo et al., 2002), the GTPase activating protein IQGAP (Watanabe et al., 2004), the guanine nucleotide exchange factor ASEF (Kawasaki et al., 2000), and the plus ends of polymerizing microtubules (Bahmanyar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jimbo et al., 2002.

claim: APC binding partners include the GTPase activating protein IQGAP.
source: In addition to binding to Dlg1, APC binding partners include the kinesin KAP3 (Jimbo et al., 2002), the GTPase activating protein IQGAP (Watanabe et al., 2004), the guanine nucleotide exchange factor ASEF (Kawasaki et al., 2000), and the plus ends of polymerizing microtubules (Bahmanyar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Watanabe et al., 2004.

claim: APC binding partners include the guanine nucleotide exchange factor ASEF.
source: In addition to binding to Dlg1, APC binding partners include the kinesin KAP3 (Jimbo et al., 2002), the GTPase activating protein IQGAP (Watanabe et al., 2004), the guanine nucleotide exchange factor ASEF (Kawasaki et al., 2000), and the plus ends of polymerizing microtubules (Bahmanyar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kawasaki et al., 2000.

claim: APC binding partners include the plus ends of polymerizing microtubules.
source: In addition to binding to Dlg1, APC binding partners include the kinesin KAP3 (Jimbo et al., 2002), the GTPase activating protein IQGAP (Watanabe et al., 2004), the guanine nucleotide exchange factor ASEF (Kawasaki et al., 2000), and the plus ends of polymerizing microtubules (Bahmanyar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bahmanyar et al., 2009.

claim: Dlg1-mediated changes in the subcellular localization of APC or in the interaction of APC with its protein partners could reduce APC-dependent beta-catenin destruction, thereby enhancing beta-catenin signaling.
source: We speculate that Dlg1-mediated changes in the subcellular localization of APC or in the interaction of APC with its protein partners could reduce APC-dependent beta-catenin destruction, thereby enhancing beta-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known functions of APC and Dlg1.

claim: Gpr124 is a seven transmembrane protein in the adhesion GPCR family that functions in concert with Reck to enhance Wnt7a/b-specific signaling through Frizzled receptors and Lrp5/6 co-receptors.
source: A second candidate for interacting with Dlg1 in the context of beta-catenin signaling in CNS ECs is Gpr124, a seven transmembrane protein in the adhesion GPCR family that functions in concert with the GPI-anchored protein Reck to enhance Wnt7a/b-specific signaling through Frizzled receptors and Lrp5/6 co-receptors (Zhou and Nathans, 2014; Posokhova et al., 2015; Vanhollebeke et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2017; Eubelen et al., 2018; Vallon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Gpr124 plays a major role in angiogenesis and vascular barrier development in the brain.
source: Gpr124 plays a major role in angiogenesis and vascular barrier development in the brain (Kuhnert et al., 2010; Anderson et al., 2011; Cullen et al., 2011) and a minor role in angiogenesis and vascular barrier development in the retina (Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuhnert et al., 2010; Anderson et al., 2011; Cullen et al., 2011.

claim: Gpr124 plays a minor role in angiogenesis and vascular barrier development in the retina.
source: Gpr124 plays a major role in angiogenesis and vascular barrier development in the brain (Kuhnert et al., 2010; Anderson et al., 2011; Cullen et al., 2011) and a minor role in angiogenesis and vascular barrier development in the retina (Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: Deletion of the Gpr124 PDZ binding motif or most of the Gpr124 intracellular domain impairs beta-catenin signaling by only approximately 20–40% in transfected cells.
source: However, deletion of the Gpr124 PDZ binding motif or most of the Gpr124 intracellular domain impairs beta-catenin signaling by only ~20–40% in transfected cells (Posokhova et al., 2015; Vallon et al., 2018), and Dlg1 co-transfection produces only a ~1.5x stimulation of Wnt7a/Fz/Gpr124/Reck signaling in STF cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Posokhova et al., 2015 and Vallon et al., 2018, and data in Figure 6E.

claim: Late gestation Dlg1-/- fetuses exhibit mis-orientation of the stereociliary bundles in inner ear sensory hair cells.
source: Late gestation Dlg1-/- fetuses exhibit (i) mis-orientation of the stereociliary bundles in inner ear sensory hair cells, (ii) defects in the closure of the palate, neural tube, and eyelids, and (iii) multiple cardiac defects, including ventricular septal defect, persistent truncus arteriosus, and double outlet right ventricle (Rivera et al., 2013; Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rivera et al., 2013 and Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2015.

claim: Late gestation Dlg1-/- fetuses exhibit defects in the closure of the palate, neural tube, and eyelids.
source: Late gestation Dlg1-/- fetuses exhibit (i) mis-orientation of the stereociliary bundles in inner ear sensory hair cells, (ii) defects in the closure of the palate, neural tube, and eyelids, and (iii) multiple cardiac defects, including ventricular septal defect, persistent truncus arteriosus, and double outlet right ventricle (Rivera et al., 2013; Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rivera et al., 2013 and Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2015.

claim: Late gestation Dlg1-/- fetuses exhibit multiple cardiac defects, including ventricular septal defect, persistent truncus arteriosus, and double outlet right ventricle.
source: Late gestation Dlg1-/- fetuses exhibit (i) mis-orientation of the stereociliary bundles in inner ear sensory hair cells, (ii) defects in the closure of the palate, neural tube, and eyelids, and (iii) multiple cardiac defects, including ventricular septal defect, persistent truncus arteriosus, and double outlet right ventricle (Rivera et al., 2013; Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rivera et al., 2013 and Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2015.

claim: The Dlg1-/- phenotypes are present in various combinations in Fz3-/-;Fz6-/-, Fz1-/-;Fz2-/- and Fz2-/-;Fz7-/- double mutant fetuses.
source: In various combinations, these defects are precisely the ones present in the following double mutant fetuses: Fz3-/-;Fz6-/-, Fz1-/-;Fz2-/- and Fz2-/-;Fz7-/- (Wang et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2012.

claim: The similarities between Dlg1-/- and Frizzled double mutant phenotypes suggest that they result from disruptions in the same signaling pathway.
source: The similarities between Dlg1-/- and these Frizzled double mutant phenotypes suggest that they result from disruptions in the same signaling pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic similarities.

claim: The Dlg1-/- phenotypes have been interpreted as reflecting a defect in planar cell polarity signaling.
source: More specifically, the Dlg1-/- phenotypes have been interpreted as reflecting a defect in planar cell polarity signaling (Rivera et al., 2013; Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rivera et al., 2013 and Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2015.

claim: Fz3 and Fz6 appear to be devoted exclusively to planar cell polarity signaling, as judged by their asymmetric subcellular localization and their failure to activate beta-catenin signaling in cell culture.
source: This interpretation could account for those phenotypes referable to reduced signaling by Fz3 and Fz6, two Frizzleds that appear to be devoted exclusively to planar cell polarity signaling, as judged by their asymmetric subcellular localization and their failure to activate beta-catenin (i.e. canonical Wnt) signaling in cell culture (Wang et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006 and Yu et al., 2012.

claim: Current evidence suggests that Fz1, Fz2, and Fz7 can transduce both planar polarity and beta-catenin signals.
source: However, this interpretation may be incomplete for those phenotypes referable to reduced signaling by Fz1, Fz2, and Fz7, as current evidence suggests that this Frizzled subfamily can transduce both planar polarity and beta-catenin signals (Lhomond et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lhomond et al., 2012 and Yu et al., 2012.

claim: Dlg1-/- fetuses exhibit defects in renal and urogenetial development that are partially overlapping with defects caused by knockout of Wnt4.
source: Additionally, Dlg1-/- fetuses exhibit defects in renal and urogenetial development that are partially overlapping with defects caused by knockout of Wnt4, further suggestive of a link to beta-catenin signaling (Vainio et al., 1999; Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vainio et al., 1999 and Iizuka-Kogo et al., 2007.

claim: It is reasonable to suggest that Dlg1 enhances beta-catenin signaling in other biological contexts and that part of the Dlg1-/- phenotype reflects this activity.
source: In light of the evidence presented here that Dlg1 enhances beta-catenin signaling in CNS ECs, it seems reasonable to suggest that Dlg1 enhances beta-catenin signaling in other biological contexts and that part of the Dlg1-/- phenotype reflects this activity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings in CNS ECs.
